age: 41
gender: male
history: A 41 year old gentleman known to have bronchiectasis presents with 4 day history of cough with purulent sputum, shortness of breath and haemoptysis.

note if they are clear despite the presence of cardiac silhouette enlargement.", "Correlate the anatomical finding (widened left superior mediastinum) with the physiological symptom (hypoxaemia) by considering a Persistent Left Superior Vena Cava (PLSVC) draining into the left atrium.", "Distinguish this from left heart failure (which would typically show pulmonary venous congestion) or compressive masses (which would not inherently cause shunting/hypoxaemia without airway compromise)."]}, {"category": "reasoning", "trigger": "When evaluating a chest X-ray showing complete opacification (white-out) of a hemithorax accompanied by a mediastinal shift.", "steps": ["Confirm the presence of total opacification on one side and identify the direction of the tracheal and cardiac silhouette shift relative to the opacity.", "If the mediastinum is shifted contralaterally (away from the opacity), diagnose a space-occupying lesion such as a massive pleural effusion or tension pneumothorax; distinguish between them by noting that effusions appear radiopaque (white) while pneumothorax appears radiolucent (black).", "If the mediastinum is shifted ipsilaterally (towards the opacity), diagnose volume loss causes such as lung collapse, atelectasis, or fibrosis.", "Rule out consolidation (pneumonia) as a primary cause for significant mediastinal shift, as it typically preserves lung volume or causes only minimal shift unless associated with substantial collapse."]}, {"category": "characterization", "trigger": "When evaluating a chest X-ray for diaphragmatic abnormalities or suspected mediastinal/diaphragmatic masses (e.g., lymphangioma).", "steps": ["Inspect the contour and position of both hemidiaphragms, specifically looking for asymmetric elevation (often right-sided) and scalloped or lobulated margins (often left-sided).", "Systematically evaluate the costophrenic angles and lung bases to confirm the absence of pleural effusion (no meniscus sign or homogeneous basal opacity), distinguishing this pattern from effusion-related diaphragmatic obscuration."]}]
